summary: Defines a MIB module for managing HDSL2 and SHDSL digital subscriber line interfaces. It extends objects and textual conventions from RFC 3276, which it replaces. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A remote dashboard for checking on certain high-speed phone-line internet connections.

questions: what is the hdsl2 shdsl mib
how does snmp monitor a dsl line
subtitle: The SNMP management objects for watching and configuring HDSL2 and SHDSL digital subscriber lines.

tldr.problem: Operators who run HDSL2 and SHDSL lines need a standard way to configure them, read their status and error statistics, and receive alarms over SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the HDSL2-SHDSL-LINE-MIB module: tables for span configuration, inventory, endpoint status, 15-minute and 1-day performance history, maintenance and shared profiles, plus threshold and fault notifications.
tldr.outcome: It replaces RFC 3276 by adding support for G.shdsl.bis and extra objects for managing SHDSL lines, and it recommends SNMPv3 security.

today: RFC 4319 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It replaced RFC 3276.

sections.title: What the MIB Module Covers
sections.content:
A MIB (Management Information Base) is a set of managed objects, normally accessed through SNMP. This RFC defines a MIB module for managing High Bit-Rate DSL 2nd generation (HDSL2) and Single-Pair High-Speed DSL (SHDSL) lines. The objects are based on the Embedded Operations Channel (EOC) specifications in ANSI T1E1.4/2000-006 and ITU G.991.2.

It obsoletes RFC 3276. The new module supports G.shdsl.bis as described in G.991.2 and adds objects to improve the management of SHDSL lines. It sits under MIB-2 transmission and is written in SMIv2.
sections.eli5: It is a long list of questions you can ask a high-speed phone-line modem, such as how fast is it and is it having trouble, along with some settings you can change.

sections.title: Line Topology and Interface Integration
sections.content:
A line has at least two units: the central-site xtuC and the remote-site xtuR. It may optionally have up to 8 repeater (regenerator) units, xru1 to xru8, between them. The whole chain is a span and each hop is a segment. Every unit has a network side and a customer side, and a line uses wire pair 1, with optional further pairs for SHDSL.

The module plugs into the standard interfaces MIB of RFC 2863. IANA assigned the ifTypes hdsl2 (168) and shdsl (169). The ifFixedLengthGroup MUST be supported, ifRcvAddressGroup does not apply, ifPhysAddress MUST be a zero-length octet string, and table entries indexed by ifIndex MUST be persistent. For HDSL2 lines, ifSpeed is fixed at 1552000.
sections.eli5: A line is like a chain of relay runners. There is one at each end and possibly a few in between, and the dashboard can ask each one how it is doing.

sections.title: Groups, Tables and Profiles
sections.content:
The module is split into groups, each with its own table: span configuration, span status, unit inventory, segment endpoint configuration, current status and performance, 15-minute interval history, 1-day interval history, maintenance (loopbacks and similar), span configuration profiles and endpoint alarm configuration profiles. Further groups cover notifications, SHDSL wire-pair status and payload rates that exclude framing overhead.

Because a managed node may handle hundreds or thousands of lines that are mostly provisioned alike, the module uses profiles: sets of parameters shared by many lines. Changing a profile reconfigures every line that refers to it, and a profile must be unreferenced from all lines before it is deleted. Implementations MUST provide a default profile named DEFVAL for each profile type. Profile changes MUST take effect immediately and MAY restart the units.
sections.eli5: Instead of setting every modem by hand, you write a settings card once, such as silver, and point many modems at it. Edit the card and all of them follow.

sections.title: Counters, Interval Buckets and Thresholds
sections.content:
For SNR margin, loop attenuation, errored seconds (ES), severely errored seconds (SES), CRC anomalies, loss of sync word (LOSW) and unavailable seconds (UAS), the module keeps event counters, a current 15-minute bucket with 0 to 96 historical 15-minute buckets, and a current 1-day counter with 0 to 30 previous days. Each current 15-minute bucket has an associated threshold notification.

There is no way to mark a bucket invalid. If the data for an interval is suspect, the agent MUST NOT report that interval, which leaves holes in the table, and notifications based on an invalid current bucket MUST NOT be generated. Counters are not reset when a unit is reinitialized, only when the agent is reset or reinitialized.
sections.eli5: The modem keeps a tally of hiccups for each 15-minute slice and for each day, like a notebook of how bumpy each hour was. It skips a page rather than write down numbers it does not trust.

sections.title: Notifications
sections.content:
Agents are required to be able to send the standard coldStart, warmStart, linkUp and linkDown notifications. The module adds its own, including loop attenuation and SNR margin crossings, threshold notifications for ES, SES, CRC anomalies, LOSW and UAS, and fault notifications such as loopback failure, device fault, configuration or protocol initialization failure, no neighbor present and local power loss.

A threshold notification fires when the current 15-minute counter becomes equal to or exceeds the threshold, and only one SHOULD be sent per interval per interface. Setting a threshold to 0 disables its notification. Setting it to 1 gives a notification on the first event, at most once every 15 minutes. Other notifications SHOULD be rate limited to at least a 1-minute gap between consecutive notifications of the same event, and throttled notifications are dropped, not queued.
sections.eli5: The modem can tap you on the shoulder when too many hiccups happen in a short time. It will not pester you more than once per slice, and you can turn the taps off.

sections.title: Compatibility With RFC 3276 Managers
sections.content:
A management application written for RFC 3276 could mistakenly flag a G.shdsl.bis unit that reports a wire pair or rate outside the old ranges. For example, a four-pair line would report statistics for pairs that do not exist in RFC 3276, so a GET-NEXT on hdsl2ShdslEndpointCurrAtn.1.1.1.2 might return hdsl2ShdslEndpointCurrAtn.1.1.1.3. Managers meant for G.shdsl.bis agents SHOULD be modified to accept this.

An unmodified manager can still manage such agents, but only up to G.SHDSL (non-bis) limits: two wire pairs and an upper rate of 4112000 bits per second.
sections.eli5: An old remote control may not know about new buttons on a newer gadget. It still works for the old buttons, but you need the new remote to use the rest.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Many objects are read-write or read-create, and the RFC lists the sensitive ones table by table. Unauthorized changes could, for example, activate a loopback and block end-to-end data transfer, raise power backoff and increase bundle interference, trigger a soft restart that briefly interrupts traffic, or alter profiles and so change alarms and notifications.

Reading is also sensitive. The inventory table exposes vendor, model, serial number and software version, which tells an intruder what equipment is in use.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. The RFC RECOMMENDS implementers use the SNMPv3 security features, including its cryptographic authentication and privacy, and says deploying versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED. Operators are responsible for giving access only to principals with legitimate rights.
sections.eli5: Anyone who can use the dashboard could switch off a customer's connection or learn which brand of modem you use, so only the right people should get in, and the channel should be locked.

items.title: Span configuration profile
items.text: Parameters for a whole span; optional for HDSL2 because they only apply to SHDSL.

items.title: DEFVAL
items.text: Reserved default profile name every implementation MUST provide.
